findings.title: Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down on first rebalance, silently dropping messages afterwards
findings.body:
The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory `__init__`. Every strategy from `create_with_partitions` reuses it, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and stops the workers.

Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation, so after the first rebalance the next strategy gets a dead pool. `work_queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit` catches it and marks the offset as completed. As a result every subsequent message is skipped without being processed, yet its offset is committed. This is silent data loss.

The pool should be owned by the strategy (created per `create_with_partitions`), or the strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool.

findings.title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread
findings.body:
`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function` there, which invokes the Arroyo `Commit` callable. That callable stages offsets on the `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`, which are single-threaded and not thread-safe. This races with `poll`/`stage_offsets` on the main thread.

It can also commit offsets for partitions that were already revoked, because the commit thread and workers keep running during a rebalance. Offsets should be collected in the background but committed from the strategy's `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread.

findings.title: Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim
findings.body:
Each `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow group therefore lets its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, so memory grows unbounded.

The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and reject or pause when they are full.

findings.title: Commits stall permanently on natural Kafka offset gaps
findings.body:
`get_committable_offsets` stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control markers and compacted topics both leave gaps. Any such gap means the committed offset never advances past it, even though every received message is processed.

The result is ever-growing reported lag and full reprocessing on restart. The contiguity check should only consider offsets that were actually received, for example by advancing to the minimum outstanding offset minus 1, or to the max seen when nothing is outstanding.

findings.title: close() stops committing before workers drain, so processed work is never committed
findings.body:
`close()` first sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread. Only after that does it shut down the pool, which lets workers finish their remaining queued items. There is no final commit.

Items completed during that drain, plus anything completed in the last second before shutdown, are never committed. They get reprocessed after every rebalance or restart. Drain the workers first, then perform one final commit.

findings.title: Failed processing still marks offset complete; docstring claims commit only after success
findings.body:
The `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raised, so failed messages are committed. That contradicts the class guarantee "Only commits offsets after successful processing".

Either the behavior or the documentation should change.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting implementation; passes only by timing
findings.body:
In `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, the worker completes offsets in `finally` even on exceptions. Offsets 100 and 101 therefore become committable and are committed on the next 1s tick of the commit loop.

The test asserts that no commit happened, and it only passes because it checks before the commit loop fires. That makes it flaky. It also contradicts its own docstring, which says errors should not block commits.
